full_judgment:
13. The High Court Division observed that the writ petitioners, finding no other alternative, compelled to appear in the second viva-voce examination. If the petitioners were successful in the second viva voce examination, they would not have filed the writ petitions. When they failed to qualify in the examination they came up with the plea that they were compelled to appear in the viva-voce examination. This proved that they accepted the decision of the PSC and sat in the second viva-voce examination and that the decision of the PSC was taken on the basis of the materials then available with it. Thus the writ petitioners not only waived but also relinquished their claim by being appeared in the second viva-voce examination by their conduct in circumstances similar to those acquired to constitute estoppel. They had forgone what they are entitled to, if any, by their conduct. The reason assigned by the High Court Division is not a legal ground to escape from the principles of estoppel. This view finds support in Suneeta Agarwal vs State of Haryana, (2000) 2 SCC 615. 

 24. Thus, there is no gainsaying the fact that a legitimate expectation would arise when a body of representation or by past practice around expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfill. Therefore, in order to claim such right the writ petitioners must satisfy that there is a foundation to make such a claim. It must also be shown that the decision taken by the PSC was arbitrary, unreasonable and not in the public interest. In the present case the decision was taken for the public interest as there was wide spread allegation that the process of recruitment was tainted by irregularities and corruption. One of the members of the PSC was facing criminal prosecution and six members had resigned. Considering that aspect of the matter, the Commission with a view to restore public confidence took the decision; the Courts cannot interfere with such a decision.
